question: Nearly shared: both papers ask whether routine non-cognitive tabular data can discriminate AACD-defined MCI (a cognition score >= 1 SD below the age-band mean) from non-MCI among Chinese community-dwelling older adults in CHARLS, using a random forest. Two judgements under condition 1 decide the case. (a) Population: P-27 restricts the sample to adults >= 60 with depression (CESD-10 >= 10), a condition that itself lowers cognitive scores, while P-96 screens general older adults. The depressed group is a subset of the same community population, not a separate disease population, but it is a comorbidity-defined population. (b) Channel: P-27's predictors are all questionnaire and self-report items (education, household registration, loneliness, IADL, diabetes, hypertension, exercise). P-96's are education plus physical examination (grip strength, height, weight) and routine blood values (creatinine, MCV, platelets). Both are clinical tabular data and share education, which is P-96's top SHAP feature, but P-96 adds anthropometric, motor and blood measures.

figures.P-27: RF AUC, reported 95% CIs: training 0.826 [0.809, 0.843]; internal validation (30% hold-out of 1964 CHARLS 2018 participants) 0.801 [0.760, 0.841]; 5-fold CV within training, mean 0.791 [0.771, 0.810]; external CLHLS 2018 (n = 6782, 1146 MCI) 0.653 [0.636, 0.670].
figures.P-96: RF AUROC, reported 95% CIs: 'Training Set' (CHARLS 2015, n = 2932, 518 MCI, stratified 5-fold CV) 0.93 [0.91, 0.95]; External Set 1 (Yiwu 2021, n = 4140) 0.83 [0.82, 0.84]; External Set 2 (CHARLS 2011, n = 1782) 0.87 [0.86, 0.88].

matched_figure_check: Neither paper reports the other's population or predictor set, so no matched-condition figure removes those differences. On the validation tier, every matched pair keeps the gap. Development/training: 0.826 [0.809, 0.843] vs 0.93 [0.91, 0.95]. Within-training 5-fold CV: 0.791 [0.771, 0.810] vs 0.93 [0.91, 0.95]. External: 0.653 [0.636, 0.670] vs 0.83 [0.82, 0.84] and 0.87 [0.86, 0.88]. The record's figures (0.826 and 0.93) are both development-set values, but the gap holds on the like-for-like external figures, so no matched figure reconciles the pair.
performance_validity: Not triggered. Neither value reaches 0.97 (maximum 0.93), and both papers report external validation.

candidate_explanations.difference: Population restricted to depressed older adults in P-27 (a restricted, comorbidity-defined sample, where depression itself depresses cognitive scores), against general older adults in P-96.
candidate_explanations.quote: The inclusion criteria for participants in both datasets were consistent: 1. Age ≥60 years; 2. Complete cognitive dimension-related data; 3. Complete depression scale responses; 4. Patients with depression.

candidate_explanations.difference: Different predictor sets: self-report and questionnaire variables (P-27) against physical-examination and routine blood variables (P-96).
candidate_explanations.quote: Ultimately, eight discriminative variables were identified: education, household registration, loneliness, IADL, diabetes, hypertension, and exercise.
Seven key variables (education, grip strength, height, weight, creatinine, mean corpuscular volume, and platelet count) were selected through majority voting.

candidate_explanations.difference: Different cognition instrument behind the AACD label: the CHARLS HRS-style battery in P-27's development data against an MMSE-based score in P-96.
candidate_explanations.quote: CHARLS evaluate cognitive performance using the identical methodological framework adopted by the U.S. Health and Retirement Study
Participants scoring ≥1 SD below their age group’s mean MMSE were classified as having cognitive impairment consistent.

candidate_explanations.difference: External cohorts differ. P-27 validates on CLHLS, whose cognition is scored with the CMMSE rather than the CHARLS battery used to train the model, a shift that may depress P-27's external AUC. P-96 validates on Yiwu 2021 and an earlier CHARLS wave (2011).
candidate_explanations.quote: CLHLS assesses cognition with the Chinese version of the Mini- Mental State Examination (CMMSE)

candidate_explanations.difference: P-96's headline 0.93 is a development ('training set') figure. Its threshold metrics imply class-balanced evaluation data: PPV 0.851 at sensitivity 0.906 and specificity 0.85 corresponds to about 50% prevalence, whereas the training set's MCI prevalence is 17.7%, which would give PPV of about 0.57. The development AUROC may therefore be optimistic, but the external AUROCs still exceed P-27's.
candidate_explanations.quote: The model demonstrated strong discrimination and calibration, with an AUROC of 0.93 on the training set, 0.83 on external validation set 1, and 0.87 on set 2.

candidate_explanations.difference: Different CHARLS waves (2018 against 2015) with likely participant overlap, so the two samples are not independent.
candidate_explanations.quote: Data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) 2015 were used to develop the model.

reason: Conditions 2 to 6 hold. Both report AUC. No matched figure reconciles the pair: the gap persists at training, cross-validation and external tiers. The reported 95% intervals do not overlap at any tier, neither result is near ceiling, and the record's figures are printed values (both development-set, with the gap confirmed on the external figures). The case turns on condition 1: whether a depression-restricted sample is the same population class as general community older adults, and whether P-96's physical-exam and blood predictors share P-27's clinical/questionnaire channel. If the operator reads both as the same class and channel, the pair is an unresolved discrepancy with the explanations listed, none shown by either paper to be sufficient. If not, it fails condition 1.

quotes.quote: In internal testing, the random forest (RF) achieved the best predictive performance (AUC = 0.826 in training and 0.801 in internal validation)
In the validation set, RF (0.801, 95 % CI: 0.760–0.841) showed a higher AUC value compared to other ML models
with a mean AUC of 0.791 (95 % CI: 0.771–0.810)
Using the cohort from CLHLS for external validation, the AUC (0.653, 95 % CI: 0.636–0.670) of RF did not reach the level of the validation set
the RF model showed the best performance, with an AUROC of 0.93[95 %CI, 0.91–0.95] and an AUPRC of 0.93 [95 %CI, 0.91–0.95].
For External Set 1, the Random Forest model achieved an AUROC of 0.83 (95 % CI: 0.82–0.84)
On External Set 2, which served as a temporal validation cohort, the AUROC further improved to 0.87 (95 % CI: 0.86–0.88)
All models were trained on the training set using stratified 5-fold cross-validation to optimize performance and reduce overfitting.
Although the model performed well on the training set, a modest decrease in performance was observed in external validation (AUROC = 0.83 and 0.87), which may reflect a dataset shift.
